intro: New in OpenTax, newest first. Each release's git tag also lists every rule that changed, with old and new amounts.

posts.title: Business losses through AGI: § 461(l) and the § 172 NOL with the 80% limit

blocks.text: Large business losses, K-1 losses and NOL carryovers now flow through AGI, taxable income and the AMT for 2025, 2026 and 2027.

items: **Excess business loss (§ 461(l), Form 461 → Schedule 1 line 8p):**

blocks.text: - Counts Schedule C/F results (both spouses), nonpassive K-1 ordinary business income and loss (new `k1OrdinaryBusinessLoss`), and Schedule E rentals when they are a trade or business. Wages never count. - Thresholds: $313,000 / $626,000 joint for 2025, $256,000 / $512,000 for 2026, $264,000 / $528,000 for 2027. Only a joint return doubles. - The disallowed amount is added back as other income and carried forward as an NOL.

items: **NOL deduction (§ 172, Schedule 1 line 8a):**

blocks.text: - Pre-2018 carryovers are deducted in full. - Post-2017 carryovers are limited to 80% of taxable income figured without the NOL deduction and § 199A. - That base is the return evaluated without the deduction, so Social Security, phase-outs and the medical floor are figured on AGI before it.

items: **NOL generated this year (Form 172 Part I, line 24),** with the nonbusiness-deduction limit, the capital loss add-back and the senior deduction left out (§ 172(d)(3)).

**Carryovers to next year (§ 172(b)(2)),** pre-2018 and post-2017 separately, oldest losses first, with the 20% reduction. Each pool's modified taxable income is the return re-run without the § 1211(b) deduction and without its own and later NOLs, so Social Security and the other AGI-dependent items are refigured as the Form 172 instructions direct. Post-2017 includes this year's NOL and excess business loss.

**AMT:** Form 6251 line 2e adds the NOL deduction back. Line 2f takes the alternative tax NOL deduction (new `alternativeTaxNolDeduction`), limited to 90% of AMTI. It is asked only with NOL carryovers when AMTI before it is above the exemption; at or below it the AMT is zero either way.
**`compute_return`** shows a `losses` block in a loss year: lines 8a and 8p, the Form 172 NOL and both carryovers.
**Asked only when it changes the answer:**

blocks.text: - whether a Schedule E activity is a trade or business; - whether the capital items are investments (only with capital gains); - an itemizer's business share of itemized deductions in a possible NOL year.

items: **Refuses, with the reason:**

blocks.text: - business capital gains or losses (Form 4797 is not modeled); - an NOL from an excess business loss, when some is deducted alongside QBI (Reg. § 1.199A-3(b)(1)(v)); - a loss year with Schedule 1-A tips, overtime or car-loan deductions, other adjustments or a § 1202 gain; - the California renter's credit when federal AGI carries an NOL or excess business loss (it uses California AGI, which follows California's own NOL rules; CalEITC and the YCTC use federal AGI and are unaffected).

items: **Checked:**

blocks.text: - The derived cases and every applicable IRS example: Form 461 (2026 draft) $94,000; the Form 172 instructions' $1 million example ($687,000 at the 2025 threshold, since the printed $738,000 uses 2021's); the Pub 536 Worksheet 1 structure. - An independent rebuild from the sources without reading this code, on 22 scenarios plus probes. It found the carryover not refiguring Social Security, line 2f skipped when the regular deduction was zero, and three questions asked when they couldn't change the answer. All are fixed and now match. - A differential against the released engine on 1,600 random returns (17,600 values). Every difference is a return with an excess business loss or one of its new questions.

posts.title: Form 4562: depreciation, § 179 and bonus, with cost-segregation classes

blocks.text: `opentax form4562` (MCP `compute_form_4562`, library `composeForm4562`) computes Form 4562 for 2025, 2026 and 2027.

- It covers the phase-out, the married-filing-separately split (50% unless elected), the business income limitation with carryover (current elections first, the disallowed part spread equally), § 179 from Schedules K-1, the SUV cap, and qualified real property. - Basis drops by the amount elected, even the part carried over (Reg. §§ 1.179-1(f), 1.179-3(f)). - Land improvements are not § 179 property. When § 179 is in play, 15- and 20-year property and asset class 57.1 need `section1245Property`.

items: **Special allowance (bonus):**

blocks.text: - 100% for property acquired after January 19, 2025 (the binding-contract date, OBBBA § 70301). - 40% in 2025 and 20% in 2026 for earlier acquisitions (60% and 40% for long-production property), and none in 2027. - The TY2025 election to take 40% instead, and election out by class (qualified improvement property is class 15).

items: **MACRS:**

blocks.text: - The printed Publication 946 tables, the ones filed returns use. - Half-year, or mid-quarter when more than 40% of the year's basis (after § 179, before bonus) went into service in the last three months; mid-month for buildings. - 150% DB, straight-line and ADS elections; earlier years' assets; dispositions during the year.

items: **Listed property:** ADS at 50% or less business use. Passenger automobile limits for cars placed in service 2020 through 2026, scaled by business use, with § 179 elected counting against the limit. A new car with 100% bonus gets the first-year limit.
**Cost segregation:** Rev. Proc. 87-56 asset classes (Pub 946 Table B-1/B-2) set the GDS and ADS periods.
**Missing facts** (acquisition date, an earlier asset's convention or bonus taken, business income) return `NEEDS_FACTS` (exit 2) with every missing item listed.
**Refuses, with the reason:**

blocks.text: - short or fiscal years and general asset accounts; - a disposition in an asset's last recovery year; - 2027 cars, whose limits aren't published; - later years of a car that took 100% bonus (Rev. Proc. 2019-13); - § 280F recapture; - § 179 elected above the dollar limit, since which asset to cut is the taxpayer's call.

items: **Checked:**

blocks.text: - Every worked example in Pub 946 and the Form 4562 instructions that applies (23 cases, 43 values). - Every table column sums to 100.00. - An independent rebuild written from the sources without reading this code, on 850 random portfolios and 84 targeted probes. It found land improvements counted as § 179 property, an election out of class 15 that missed qualified improvement property, the car limit counting § 179 deducted instead of elected, and four refusals the sources answer. All are fixed. Every portfolio both sides compute now agrees to the cent, except line 2 on returns with no § 179, which this build leaves informational.

posts.title: Projection: tax years 2028 to 2035 at an inflation rate you choose

blocks.text: `--project-inflation 2.5` on `eval`, `check` and the solver commands, or `projection: { inflationPercent }` on the MCP tax tools, computes a year after 2027. Without it, 2028 and later still refuse.

items: **Method:** every inflation-adjusted amount is carried forward by its own statutory formula. That is the base amount × the index ratio, rounded the way its section says: down to $25 or $50, to the nearest $10 or $100, rounding the increase or the whole amount.

blocks.text: - The 2027 index is the one the IRS used: the C-CPI-U for September 2025 to August 2026 as first published, an 11-month average because October 2025 was never published, over each base year's index under § 1(f)(3). - For 2028 on, that index grows by your rate each year. - The wage base and the household employee threshold follow the wage index instead, at `--project-wage-growth` (default: the inflation rate). The wage base never falls.

items: **Checked:** the formula and data reproduce all 76 indexed amounts in the 2027 rules exactly, along with the published 2025 and 2026 amounts. The one exception is the IRS's 2026 head-of-household standard deduction ($24,150), which departs from § 63(c)(7)(B)(ii)'s rounding; 2027 follows the statute, and projections start from the statutory base.

blocks.text: - Every amount in the 49 rules that change each year is classified as indexed, derived from an indexed amount (joint = 200%, MFS = 50%, the EITC maximums and phase-out ends, the Schedule AI wage-base fractions), set by law, or a fixed constant. A test fails if one isn't.

items: **Law, not projection:**

blocks.text: - The SALT limit and threshold rise 101% a year through 2029 (to the cent; the statute gives no rounding), and the limit is $10,000 from 2030. - The tips, overtime, car-loan and senior deductions end after 2028.

items: **Refuses rather than guesses:**

blocks.text: - The premium tax credit, whose percentages follow premium growth, not prices. - Whatever 2027 itself refuses (IRA, SEP and saver's contributions, mileage). - States.

items: **Labeled:** every projected rule cites "PROJECTION, NOT PUBLISHED LAW" and the assumed rates. Answers carry a `projected` block. The corpus version names the year and rates (for example `0.46.0+projected.2030.cpi-2.5.awi-2.5`), so `opentax verify` rebuilds the same corpus and checks the proof.
**Library:** `getProjectedFederalCorpus({ year, inflationPercent, wageGrowthPercent })` returns a corpus to evaluate against, and the published corpus is untouched.

posts.title: Form 2210: the estimated tax penalty, with Schedule AI for every income type

blocks.text: `opentax form2210` (MCP `compute_form_2210`, library `composeForm2210`) computes Form 2210 for 2025, 2026 and 2027.

items: **Part I:** the required annual payment, from the engine's own line 22, other taxes and refundable credits.

blocks.text: - It is the smaller of 90% of this year's tax and 100% of last year's. Last year's counts at 110% when last year's AGI was over $150,000, or $75,000 married filing separately. - The $1,000 tests apply. - With no prior-year return, line 9 is line 5.

items: **Part III:** Section A per installment, then the penalty worksheet.

blocks.text: - Payments go first to the earliest underpayment. A payment can pay a column's underpayment only if it was made after that column's due date. - Withholding counts as paid one-fourth on each due date (§ 6654(g)), and like any payment it pays the earliest underpayment still open. The printed worksheet keeps withholding off line 1b, which charges the same dollars twice when withholding covers an earlier quarter; the penalty here follows the statute. - Box D (actual withholding dates) is used only when it lowers the penalty. - A payment on the next business day after a weekend due date counts as made on the due date (§ 7503). - § 6654(h) applies: no penalty on the January installment when the return is filed and the tax paid in full by January 31. The payment with the return counts in column (d), and the tool checks that the payments really cover the year's tax. - The penalty is the sum of the worksheet lines shown, each to the cent. A refused penalty (an unannounced quarter) comes back as `NOT_MODELED`, exit 3, with the final lines in `error.data`.

items: **Rates:** each quarter's § 6621 underpayment rate, by days over 365 (366 in a leap year). The rates come from the IRS quarterly-rates page and the Revenue Rulings it cites.

blocks.text: - 2025 Q2 through 2026 Q1: 7%. 2026 Q2: 6% (Rev. Rul. 2026-5). 2026 Q3 and Q4: 7%. - The printed 2025 worksheet uses 7% through April 15, 2026, but April 1–15 is 6%. The instructions allow any method that reaches the correct penalty, and the output says so. - A penalty that would run into a quarter whose rate isn't announced yet (2027 Q1 on) is refused. Section A is still shown.

items: **Schedule AI (box C):** pass the cumulative amounts through March 31, May 31 and August 31.

blocks.text: - Each column is the whole return computed on those amounts × 4, 2.4, 1.5 and 1, with the standard deduction in full. So every income type, deduction and credit the engine models is annualized: interest, dividends, capital gains, pensions, Social Security, itemized deductions, QBI, AMT, NIIT, Additional Medicare Tax and the credits. - The tool reports both methods and takes the lower penalty. - It refuses, with the reason, where the form doesn't settle the period treatment: the foreign earned income exclusion, prior-year carryovers, the premium tax credit, Form 8615, Schedule H, a dependent filer, and a period whose annualized state and local taxes exceed the SALT limit. - It matches the corpus's existing wage and self-employment installment rules column by column for 2025, 2026 and 2027.

items: **Checked:**

blocks.text: - The instructions' Examples 3 and 4 ($202.82 with the 6% April) and hand-worked 2025 and 2026 penalties. - An independent build of the form, written from the instructions without reading this code: 576 random returns (2025 and 2026, 204 with Schedule AI) and 20 hand-built ones. - After the fixes above, every priced penalty matches it to the cent.

posts.title: Tax year 2027

blocks.text: Federal returns now compute for tax year 2027 (`--as-of 2027-12-31`) on the published 2027 law, so a planning scenario can be carried from 2025 through 2027.

items: **Amounts and sources.** Every inflation-adjusted amount is from an official source:

blocks.text: - Rev. Proc. 2026-35 (released November 5, 2026): brackets, capital gain breakpoints, standard deduction, AMT, EITC, CTC $2,300 and ACTC $1,800, adoption credit, kiddie tax, QBI threshold and the $415 / $1,030 minimum, student loan interest, educator expenses, § 179, § 461(l), § 163(j) gross receipts, the foreign earned income exclusion, the qualifying-relative test, estate and trust brackets. - Rev. Proc. 2026-24: HSA limits, $4,500 and $9,000. - Rev. Proc. 2026-26: premium tax credit percentages, 2.15% to 10.22%, with the 2026 poverty guidelines (91 FR 1797). - SSA (91 FR 67380): wage base $192,300 and household employee threshold $3,100. - Statute: SALT is 101% of 2026 under § 164(b)(7), so $40,804 with a $510,050 threshold.

items: **Law that changes in 2027:**

blocks.text: - The saver's credit counts only ABLE-account contributions (§ 25B(d)(1) after SECURE 2.0). - The premium tax credit is limited to eligible individuals (OBBBA § 71301). The inputs attest it.

items: **Not published yet, so these refuse rather than guess:**

blocks.text: - The IRS's 2027 retirement-plan limits: a 2027 IRA, SEP/solo-401(k) or saver's contribution, and the retirement maximum targets. - The 2027 standard mileage rate. - A return with none of these computes normally.

items: **States:** they still cover 2025 and 2026 and refuse 2027 until their own 2027 amounts are published.

blocks.text: Fixes found while checking:

items: The educator expense amount is $350 for 2026 (Rev. Proc. 2025-32 § 4.12). The engine had kept 2025's $300. It stays $350 for 2027.

Gambling losses from 2026 follow § 165(d) as amended by OBBBA § 70114: 90 percent of the losses, limited to the winnings. From 2026, `gamblingLossesItemized` is the total losses for the year, and the new input `gamblingWinnings` supplies the limit. Before, the engine deducted 100 percent.

The premium tax credit's 400% cliff now compares household income to 4 × the poverty line directly. It used to compare a percentage rounded down to the cent, so income up to a few dollars over the line still got the full credit. This applies to 2026 and 2027.

The 2026 standard mileage rate is 72.5¢ before July 1 and 76¢ from July 1 (Announcement 2026-11). The new input `businessMilesDrivenFromJuly` gives the later miles. Before, every 2026 mile used 72.5¢.

Additional Medicare Tax no longer counts self-employment net earnings under $400. They are not self-employment income (§ 1402(b)), and Form 8959 line 8 takes Schedule SE line 6, which is blank in that case. This applies to every year.

posts.title: Form 6251 line by line, and no deductions from a negative AGI

blocks.text: The alternative minimum tax now follows Form 6251 line by line, and the Schedule A floors no longer turn a negative AGI into a deduction.

items: Line 13 is line 4 of the Qualified Dividends and Capital Gain Tax Worksheet: net capital gain plus qualified dividends, not limited to taxable income. Only the part of the AMT base above that amount is taxed at 26% or 28%. When net capital gain exceeded taxable income, the AMT was too high: for MFJ 2025 with $10,000 of interest and $2,000,000 of long-term gain it was $8,190, and it is now $6,900.

Line 40 now caps the tentative minimum tax at the flat 26%/28% tax on the whole base (line 39), and the 0% and 15% bands are measured as lines 19–30 do. When the AMT base is smaller than the capital gain and dividends, the whole base is taxed at the capital gain rates.

Line 1b starts from AGI less the Form 1040 line 14 deductions and can be negative, as the form says. Before, AMT income started from taxable income, which stops at zero, so a loss year with an ISO exercise overstated it.
Married filing separately adds the § 55(d)(2) amount to AMT income above $900,350 for 2025 (25% of the excess, at most $68,500) and above $640,200 for 2026 (50%, at most $70,100).
A child subject to the kiddie tax gets the full AMT exemption. § 55(d)(4)(A)(iii) turns off the § 59(j) cap for years after 2017, and the 2025 Exemption Worksheet has no such step.

Line 2a follows the deduction actually taken: a filer who elects to itemize adds back the Schedule A taxes, and a filer whose standard deduction includes a net qualified disaster loss adds back only the standard deduction before the increase. For 2026 itemizers, AMT income also allows the deductions before the § 68 limit ("Section 68 shall not apply", § 56(b)(1)(E)).
Line 10 includes Schedule 2 line 1z, so the excess advance premium tax credit repayment now reduces the AMT.

New targets for each step: `us.federal.amt.amti` (line 4), `us.federal.amt.exemption` (line 5), `us.federal.amt.taxable_excess` (line 6), `us.federal.amt.capital_gain_amount` (line 13) and `us.federal.amt.tentative_minimum_tax` (line 9).

blocks.text: When AGI is negative, the 7.5% medical floor and the 10% casualty floor treat it as zero. Before, they turned it into a deduction of up to 17.5% of the loss with no expense entered. The 60% cash charitable limit also treats a negative AGI as zero: it allows no deduction, where for 2025 it produced a negative charitable deduction.

The SALT cap for married filing separately now halves the amount after the phase-down, as § 164(b)(6)(B) and line 10 of the Schedule A worksheet do: $20,000 less 15% of modified AGI over $250,000 for 2025, never below $5,000. Before, it took 30% off $20,000 and reached the $5,000 floor at $300,000 instead of $350,000. Modified AGI now includes the § 911 foreign earned income exclusion.

The nonrefundable credits are now limited by Form 1040 line 18, which includes the excess advance premium tax credit repayment, as every credit limit worksheet says (`us.federal.tax_before_nonrefundable_credits`). The repayment moves from `us.federal.other_taxes` (Schedule 2 Part II) to that line; net tax is unchanged except where a credit was cut short by the old limit.

`us.federal.balance_due` now subtracts estimated tax payments (`federalEstimatedPayments`, Form 1040 line 26) and the extension payment (`federalExtensionPayment`, line 31) as well as withholding. Before, it subtracted withholding only. Giving any of the three now switches the CLI and MCP to the balance-due answer.
A check of every rule for the same kind of error found four more, now fixed:

items: The child and dependent care credit now reduces earned income by a Schedule C loss (Pub. 503). Before, wages alone set the limit.
Taxable Social Security now counts a Schedule C loss, pre-2019 alimony received and HSA distributions not spent on medical care in modified income, the same as AGI does.

The premium tax credit treats household income below zero as zero (Form 8962 line 3). Below 100% of the poverty line it now applies Reg. § 1.36B-2(b)(6): when the Marketplace estimated at enrollment that income would be at least 100% and advance payments were made, the credit is allowed at the lowest tier's percentage. Before, those taxpayers got no credit and repaid the advance. The engine asks `ptcEnrollmentEstimateAtLeast100Fpl` only in that case.
Oklahoma's special 65+ exemption is no longer allowed to a qualifying surviving spouse whose federal AGI is negative.

The 2026 charitable deduction for non-itemizers (§ 170(p)) is limited to 60% of AGI. § 170(p) switches off only the carryovers and the 0.5% floor, not the (b)(1)(G)(i) limit, so a negative AGI allows nothing.

posts.title: QBI per business, with aggregation

blocks.text: The § 199A deduction now follows Form 8995-A with one column per business. Above the threshold, each business gets its own W-2 wage and UBIA limit and its own SSTB status, instead of one limit for everything.

items: List up to five businesses separately with `qbiAdditionalBusinesses` and `qbiBusiness2Income` through `qbiBusiness6Income`, each with its own `W2Wages`, `UBIA`, `IsSSTB` and `AggregationGroup`. A listed business stays in the return's income: its profit is part of `selfEmploymentNetProfit` or `k1OrdinaryBusinessIncome`, and its QBI loss part of `qbiLossOffset`. Listing it only separates it for § 199A. What isn't listed is the main business, which keeps `qbiW2Wages`, `qbiUBIA` and `businessIsSSTB`.

On a joint return, the second spouse's Schedule C is its own business, with `spouseQbiW2Wages`, `spouseQbiUBIA` and `spouseBusinessIsSSTB`. Two self-employed spouses above the threshold now get a deduction instead of a refusal.
Aggregation (Schedule B): businesses with the same group number add their QBI, W-2 wages and UBIA and are limited as one. An SSTB can't be aggregated, and the engine refuses if one is.

Loss netting (Schedule C): a business's QBI loss, and last year's carryforward (`qbiLossCarryforward`), is shared among the profitable businesses in proportion to their QBI. Next year's carryforward is `us.federal.qbi.loss_carryforward`.
Each step has its own target, such as `us.federal.qbi.business2.component` or `us.federal.qbi.main.adjusted_qbi`.
A business that breaks even still brings its W-2 wages and UBIA to its aggregation group.

The 2026 $400 minimum now needs $1,000 of QBI from qualified businesses. An SSTB past the phase-in range isn't one, so it no longer gets the $400, and one within the range counts at its applicable percentage.

blocks.text: Apart from that minimum, nothing changes for a return with one business: every other existing amount is the same. Returns with business income now list two more assumptions, no businesses listed separately and no loss carryforward, so a caller that refuses defaults is asked for both.

posts.title: Retirement contribution maximums

blocks.text: New targets give the most a self-employed person or an S-corporation owner can put into a solo 401(k) or a SEP, for 2025 and 2026:

items: Sole proprietors: `us.federal.retirement.solo_401k_max.schedule_c` and `us.federal.retirement.sep_max.schedule_c`. These follow the IRS Publication 560 Deduction Worksheet for Self-Employed step by step, from net profit less half the self-employment tax.
S-corporation owners: `us.federal.retirement.solo_401k_max.s_corp` and `us.federal.retirement.sep_max.s_corp`. These start from the owner's plan compensation, `ownerEmployeePlanCompensation`.

blocks.text: Each solo 401(k) maximum is split into its employer, deferral and catch-up parts. The limits are applied per year:

items: The § 402(g) deferral limit, shared with other employers' plans through `otherElectiveDeferrals`.
Catch-up from age 50, and the higher limit at ages 60 to 63 (`isAge60Through63`).
The § 415(c) annual additions limit.
The § 401(a)(17) compensation cap.

posts.title: Self-employment tax for both spouses

blocks.text: When both spouses on a joint return are self-employed, each now gets their own Schedule SE, as the instructions require. Enter the second spouse's profit in `spouseSelfEmploymentNetProfit` and their W-2 box 3 in `spouseSocialSecurityWages` (`--spouse-se-profit`, `--spouse-ss-wages`). Both are asked only on a joint return. Each Schedule SE has its own $400 floor and its own social security wage base, so a spouse whose W-2 already reaches the base owes only the Medicare part, while the other still owes both. The two amounts add on Schedule 2 line 4 and Schedule 1 line 15, and both profits count in gross income, earned income, QBI and Form 8959. Above the § 199A threshold, two spouses' businesses refuse until per-business QBI ships.

posts.title: Net rental income in the net investment income tax

blocks.text: The 3.8% net investment income tax now counts net rental income, as Form 8960 line 4a does. Before, a passive rental's income raised AGI but never reached net investment income. A real estate professional whose rental is a trade or business, or a rental grouped with a business you materially participate in, stays out: set `rentalNotInvestmentIncome` (`--rental-not-investment-income`). The question is only asked when there is rental income.

posts.title: Form 5695 residential energy credits

blocks.text: `compute_return` now fills in Form 5695 when you give it `energy_credits` inputs: the residential clean energy credit (§ 25D, solar, battery storage, geothermal, fuel cells) and the energy efficient home improvement credit (§ 25C, insulation, doors, windows, heat pumps, energy audits), each line capped as the printed form caps it. Both credits ended after 2025, so 2026 inputs earn $0, but a 2025 clean energy carryforward still applies in 2026. The return now includes Form 1040 line 20 and Schedule 3, and the nonrefundable credits apply in the order the 2025 worksheets give.

posts.title: Capital loss carryovers, short-term and long-term

blocks.text: Two new inputs take last year's capital loss carryover: `priorYearShortTermCapitalLossCarryover` (Schedule D line 6) and `priorYearLongTermCapitalLossCarryover` (line 14). Each one nets into its own bucket before short-term and long-term are combined, the way Schedule D does it.

The carryover to next year now comes out in two parts, `us.federal.capital_loss_carryover.short_term` and `us.federal.capital_loss_carryover.long_term`, following the Capital Loss Carryover Worksheet. Enter them next year as the two new inputs. `us.federal.capital_loss_carryover` is still the total.
When taxable income is below zero, part of the $3,000 loss allowance doesn't count as used (§ 1212(b)(2)), so more of the loss carries forward. The carryover now reflects that.

posts.title: The Tax Table on capital gains returns

blocks.text: Line 22 of the Qualified Dividends and Capital Gain Tax Worksheet takes the tax on the ordinary part of your income from the Tax Table when that part is under $100,000, even when taxable income is $100,000 or more. OpenTax now does the same for 2025 and 2026, which can change the tax by a few dollars. `useFormulaMethod` still gives the exact brackets.

posts.title: New York tax table on the IT-201

blocks.text: `compute_state_return` now takes IT-201 line 39 from the New York State Tax Table when taxable income is under $65,000, as the instructions require, instead of the rate schedule. When New York AGI is over $107,650, the return lists line 39 as incomplete, because the tax computation worksheets for that range aren't encoded yet.

posts.title: Turn off defaults

blocks.text: When you leave an input out, OpenTax fills it in with a documented default and lists it under `assumptions`. A married couple with two children and a salary rests on 77 of them. You can now turn that off, so every number comes only from facts you gave.
How it works

Pass `refuseDefaults: true` to `calculate_tax` or `compute_return`, or `--refuse-defaults` on the command line. Any input you didn't give comes back under `NEEDS_FACTS`, along with the default it would have used. Answer them, or accept the ones you agree with in `allowDefaults`.
One thing to know
An unanswered question can hide the questions that depend on it, so a second call can list a few more. For the couple above, the first call lists 74 and the second lists 3.
Defaults stay on unless you ask, so existing calls work exactly as before.

posts.title: Add your own rules

blocks.text: You can now add rules of your own to OpenTax with `extendCorpus`, for things like passive losses tracked by activity or an NOL carryforward. They run alongside the federal rules and show up in the proof like any other rule.
Add to a total

A rule marked `contributesTo` adds its result to one of four totals: gross income, adjustments to income, other taxes, or refundable credits. These four keep their names and meaning from release to release, so your rules keep working as the federal rules are updated.
"Computed without regard to"

Tax law often limits a deduction based on income figured before that deduction. The 80% limit on NOLs is one. A rule can now read a total with its own contribution left out, so you can write that limit directly.
Replace a rule

To replace one of the federal rules, pin the version you built against. If a later release changes that rule, OpenTax stops and tells you which one, so you can review the change before your version runs again.
Proofs

Your rules and the federal rules share one fingerprint, and `verifyProof` checks a proof against it as usual. The [README](https://github.com/Invaro/opentax-engine/blob/main/README.md) has an example.

posts.title: See what changed in each release

blocks.text: Every release now comes with notes listing each rule that was added, removed or changed, and what changed in it: the formula, the dates it applies, the legal citation, or an amount. When an amount changes, the notes show the old and new value in dollars. You'll find them in each release's [git tag](https://github.com/Invaro/opentax-engine/tags).

posts.title: Connect your agent with one sign-in

blocks.text: There's now a second MCP address, `https://opentax.invaro.ai/mcp/account`. Add it to Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or Claude Code and the app asks you to sign in to OpenTax once, in your browser, with your email. After that, OpenTax knows which account and plan each call comes from. There's no key to copy.
Check what you're connected as
Ask your agent to call `my_account`. It answers with your email, your plan and, on the Firm plan, your firm.
Disconnect any time
Your account page lists every app you've connected, when you connected it and when it last called OpenTax. Disconnect one and it stops working right away, until you sign in again.
The open address, `https://opentax.invaro.ai/mcp`, works exactly as before, with no account.

posts.title: A new license for new releases

blocks.text: Releases from October 26, 2026 are under the Business Source License 1.1. It covers using OpenTax inside your organization, client work included. If you'd like to build it into something people outside your organization use, like a client portal, an API or an app you sell, write to founders@invaro.ai about an embedding license.

Earlier releases keep the license they shipped with, and each version becomes AGPL three years after its release. The full terms are in [LICENSE](https://github.com/Invaro/opentax-engine/blob/main/LICENSE) and [COMMERCIAL-LICENSE.md](https://github.com/Invaro/opentax-engine/blob/main/COMMERCIAL-LICENSE.md).

posts.title: Returns now say what they leave out

blocks.text: `compute_return` and `compute_state_return` now tell you when a return isn't complete. Each response has `complete: true` or `false`, and `incomplete` lists every printed line this version doesn't compute, with the form, the line, the amount involved and the reason. With `strict: true`, an incomplete return is refused with `INCOMPLETE_RETURN`.
Excess social security withholding

When two employers together withhold more social security tax than the yearly maximum, the return now lists the excess credit (Schedule 3, line 11) as not computed, with the amount. Before, it was only mentioned in a note.
States waiting on 2026 figures

Delaware, Montana, North Dakota, New Mexico, Rhode Island and Vermont now mark each line whose 2026 figure hasn't been published, instead of printing $0 next to a note. In Vermont one missing figure affects every later line, so it refuses until the figure is out.
explain_rule
`explain_rule` was returning only version information. It now returns every version of the rule with its formula, the quoted law, the rules it depends on, and its hash.

posts.title: A REST API, full proofs and whole-dollar returns

blocks.text: Every tool is now a plain REST endpoint at `/v1/tools/{tool}`, with an OpenAPI document and docs at [opentax.invaro.ai/docs](https://opentax.invaro.ai/docs). Sign in to the console for an API key and your usage.
Full proofs
Pass `includeProof: true` and the response includes the complete proof: every rule, input and rounding step, about 200 KB.
Whole dollars, like the form

`compute_return` now rounds every amount to whole dollars after adding up your documents, the way Form 1040 does, so line 15 matches its row in the Tax Table. $75,249.50 of wages now gives $8,010 of tax, not $7,999.
Strict mode
A W-2 without box 2 is noted as a $0 assumption. With `strict: true` it's refused instead, naming the missing box. W-2 box 4 is accepted too.
Six more states
Hawaii, Rhode Island, Montana, Delaware, North Dakota and Vermont now have full rules and print their form's lines.

posts.title: Nine more states

blocks.text: Connecticut, Oklahoma, Kansas, Arkansas, New Mexico, Nebraska, Idaho, West Virginia and Maine now have full rules and print their form's lines. Arkansas and Maine match their printed tax tables at every row, and Oklahoma includes its new 2026 rate schedule.

posts.title: Seven more states, and 2026 state rates

blocks.text: Maryland, Missouri, Wisconsin, Minnesota, South Carolina, Alabama and Oregon now have full rules and print their form's lines. Oregon includes its kicker credit, and Alabama its new overtime deduction. Fifteen states now answer for 2026 using their enacted rates.

posts.title: New Jersey, Ohio, Georgia and North Carolina

blocks.text: Four more states with full rules and their form's lines. A new coverage report shows which states are complete and which are waiting on published figures.

posts.title: Pennsylvania

blocks.text: Pennsylvania's PA-40, with its eight separate income classes, and the form's lines printed.

posts.title: OpenTax is public

blocks.text: The engine, the federal rules, a command line tool, and an MCP server for AI assistants. Every answer comes with a proof that cites the law behind each step.

The first release covers capital gains (Schedule D), rental depreciation, pensions under the simplified method and 1099s. It also includes rule search, and a `check` command that tells you whether a claimed amount is right.
